text: More than 2,000 years ago, the Tocharians lived in oasis cities around a great desert in today’s China.
An oasis is a watered place in a desert; theirs got water from melting mountain snow.
src: city-states by the 2nd century BCE / The oases of the northern Tarim Basin and the Turpan Depression (modern Xinjiang, China) / The Taklamakan Desert at the heart of the Tarim Basin is barren
meltwater from the surrounding mountains feeds streams that people turned into oases

text: They grew millet, wheat, rice and grapes, and raised horses, cattle, sheep and camels.
A Chinese book says their biggest city, Kucha, had triple walls and a thousand temples.
src: The people grew red millet, wheat, rice, legumes, hemp, grapes and pomegranates, and reared horses, cattle, sheep and camels
Kucha (Kuśi), the largest / The Book of Jin describes a city with threefold walls, a thousand temples and stupas

text: Their cities stood on the Silk Road, where caravans of traders passed through.
Caravans carried wooden passes telling the next station how big the caravan was.
src: oasis cities on the northern Silk Road / The oasis cities stood on the branch of the Silk Road along the northern edge of the Taklamakan
travel passes: small slips of poplar wood telling the officials at the next station along the road the size of the caravan allowed to pass

text: Most Tocharians became Buddhists, and Kucha was a centre of Buddhist learning.
The Chinese monk Xuanzang found about a hundred monasteries there, with over 5,000 monks.
src: which suggests that the Tocharians largely embraced Buddhism / From the 3rd century Kucha was a centre of Buddhist study
630: The monk Xuanzang visits Kucha and records about a hundred convents with more than five thousand monks / Buddhist monasteries of the Sarvāstivāda school

text: At the Kizil Caves, painters filled over 200 cave temples with stories of the Buddha.
They wrote their two languages in an Indian script, and one love poem survives.
src: The Kizil Caves, 65 km west of Kucha, hold over 236 Buddhist temples whose murals date from the 3rd to the 8th century. They mostly depict Jataka tales, avadanas and legends of the Buddha
Their two languages, Tocharian A and Tocharian B / The Tocharians wrote in a close variant of the Indian Middle-Brahmi script / one love poem in Tocharian B, manuscript B-496, was found at Kizil

text: More than 1,300 years ago, Chinese armies conquered their cities and killed many people in Kucha.
Their people mixed with the Uyghurs, who ruled from Gaochang, and spoke Uyghur instead.
src: they never recovered from the Tang conquest of the 640s / In 648 the general Ashina She’er took Kucha, and when its forces killed the protector-general Guo Xiaoke he had 11,000 inhabitants executed
their people blended with the Uyghurs, whose language replaced theirs / the Uyghurs founded the Kingdom of Qocho, with its capital at Gaochang near Turfan
